title: PowerShell.exe on scranton opened lsass.exe with full-access masks (0x1F3FFF / 0x1FFFFF) under user pbeesly
summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:05:16 UTC, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) on scranton.dmevals.local opened lsass.exe (PID 736) twice within 31 ms with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and 0x1FFFFF — PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS-style rights used for LSASS memory dumping, not the benign 0x1000/0x1400 query rights that dominate the 326 lsass access events. The security log independently records the same handle requests (4656, AccessMask 0x1fffff and 0x1f3fff, SubjectUserName pbeesly) plus a 4663 read (AccessMask 0x10) on \Device\HarddiskVolume2\Windows\System32\lsass.exe. This occurred in the middle of a hands-on-keyboard intrusion by pbeesly on scranton: SysinternalsSuite was unzipped and moved to C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite, accesschk.exe was run, Invoke-Discovery / Invoke-Persistence / Get-PrivateKeys were executed, and sdelete64 was used to wipe files. No .dmp file was written to disk in the window, so the dump may have been held in memory or the write was not captured.

title: wsmprovhost.exe on nashua opened lsass.exe with 0x1F3FFF during a remote PowerShell session as pbeesly
summary: On nashua.dmevals.local at 03:09:29 UTC, wsmprovhost.exe (PID 7720, the WinRM/remote PowerShell host) opened lsass.exe (PID 728) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF; the call trace runs through System.ni.dll and Microsoft.PowerShell.Commands.Management.ni.dll, i.e. the access was made from PowerShell code. The security log shows the matching 4656 handle request with AccessMask 0x1f3fff and SubjectUserName pbeesly. The script block executed one second earlier was 'Get-Process -IncludeUserName | Select-Object UserName,SessionId | Where-Object { $_.UserName -like "*\$env:USERNAME" } | Sort-Object SessionId -Unique', which is a session/user enumeration rather than a dump routine, and no dump file or dump command line was observed. The access mask is nonetheless dump-capable and the same account was dumping LSASS on scranton minutes earlier, so this is treated as suspicious rather than confirmed dumping.

title: lsass.exe wrote HKLM\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\F on scranton — normal SAM account update, not hive extraction
summary: The only registry write touching SAM\SAM in the dataset is a Sysmon event 13 at 03:19:10 UTC on scranton.dmevals.local where lsass.exe (PID 748) set HKLM\SAM\SAM\Domains\Account\F to 'Binary Data'. This is the SAM account record being updated by the LSA itself, not a reg save / esentutl / hive-copy operation: no process creation referenced reg save, esentutl or SAM (C019 zero hits), no SAM/SECURITY/SYSTEM hive file was created (C020 only matched Prefetch .pf files), and no 4663 object access on SAM/SECURITY was recorded (C024 zero hits). The 16962 event on scranton is the standard 'Remote calls to the SAM database are being restricted' policy message.

title: No NTDS.dit / shadow-copy activity observed
summary: No process creation referenced ntdsutil, vssadmin or diskshadow (C028 zero hits), no file named ntds/.dit was created (C029, C030 zero hits), no 4663 object access on ntds (C032 zero hits), no matching service/other-channel messages (C033) and no PowerShell script block referencing ntds/vssadmin/diskshadow (C034). The 12 zeek smb_files records returned no file names (C035), so no NTDS.dit transfer is visible on the wire either. Nothing in the retrieved data supports NTDS extraction.

title: No LSA secrets dumping observed; lsass image loads are Microsoft-signed system DLLs
summary: No process creation referenced SECURITY, secrets, lsadump or reg save (C036 zero hits), no 4663 object access on SECURITY\Policy\Secrets (C039 zero hits), no 4688 or 4104 referencing lsadump/secrets (C041, C042 zero hits). The 23 image-load events for lsass/samlib/vaultcli are samlib.dll ('SAM Library DLL', Microsoft Corporation) loaded into svchost.exe and powershell.exe, which is normal for SAM/LSA API use. The 4673 sensitive-privilege events involving lsass are all generated by lsass.exe itself (103 events, C014).

title: No cached domain credential dumping observed
summary: No 4663 object access on Cache/SECURITY objects (C048 zero hits) and no other-channel message referencing cachedump/mscash/Cache (C051 zero hits). The only credential-adjacent collection seen on scranton was Get-PrivateKeys exporting certificates to .pfx files under the user's Downloads folder, which is certificate theft rather than cached domain credential extraction.

title: DRSUAPI binds in zeek are DRSBind/DRSCrackNames/DRSUnbind only — no DCSync replication
summary: The zeek window (2020-04-30, which does not overlap the Windows logs) contains 9 drsuapi DCE-RPC records: DRSBind, DRSCrackNames and DRSUnbind from 10.0.1.4 and 10.0.1.6 to 10.0.0.4 (port 49667). No DRSGetNCChanges — the operation that actually replicates directory secrets in a DCSync — appears in the 123 dce_rpc operations (C018), and no process creation or script block referenced drsuapi/lsadump/dcsync (C056, C057, C058 zero hits). Name-cracking binds are consistent with normal domain name resolution, not credential replication.

title: Credential-access tooling staged on scranton by pbeesly (Sysinternals suite, accesschk, sdelete) alongside LSASS access
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local the account pbeesly ran a hands-on-keyboard intrusion between 02:56 and 03:07 UTC: SysinternalsSuite.zip was expanded and moved to C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite, accesschk.exe was executed, Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence (steps 1 and 2) and Get-PrivateKeys were invoked, screenshots and clipboard were captured, and sdelete64.exe was used to wipe C:\programdata\victim\???cod.3aka3.scr, $env:APPDATA\Draft.Zip and the SysinternalsSuite.zip. The same session produced the full-access LSASS handle requests at 03:05:16. The 4673 events show the malicious C:\ProgramData\victim\...scr and PowerShell using SeProfileSingleProcessPrivilege/SeTcbPrivilege. This is attacker credential-access activity, not normal system behaviour.

The single hit for packet-capture command lines (check C060) is on scranton.dmevals.local at 2020-05-01T23:19:17-04:00 (2020-05-02T03:19:17Z): netsh.exe 'trace start capture=yes traceFile="C:\windows\TEMP\E7116ECA-...\B91E06C5-....etl"'. The 4688 event shows the creator subject is SCRANTON$ (S-1-5-18, logon 0x3e7) and the creator process is C:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.Azure.NetworkWatcher.NetworkWatcherAgentWindows\1.4.1421.1\NetworkWatcherAgent\NetworkWatcherAgent.exe — the Azure platform's network diagnostics extension. Sysmon corroborates the same netsh capture start (SYSTEM) and a matching 'netsh.exe trace stop' 7 seconds later, plus the resulting .etl file write. This is a short, self-terminating platform capture, not a sustained promiscuous-mode sniffer. No pktmon/windump/tcpdump usage, no pcap/npcap/winpcap service installs (C062 zero hits), and no PowerShell pktmon/promisc/Get-NetAdapter activity (C063 zero hits).
title: netsh packet capture on scranton.dmevals.local is the Azure Network Watcher agent, not adversary sniffing

summary: In the zeek window (2020-04-30T00:06:38Z..00:45:00Z) the 613 conn records are dominated by ssl (378), dns (39), krb_tcp (25), dce_rpc (20) and gssapi/smb combinations; there is no ftp, telnet or ftp-data service at all, so no cleartext credential exchange was captured that a sniffer could have harvested. The 62 http records are all Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/DavClnt traffic from 10.0.1.4 to 192.168.0.4:80 performing PROPFIND/PUT/LOCK on /webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z and /webdav/python.exe — WebDAV upload/download, not authentication traffic. The only zeek notices are SSL::Invalid_Server_Cert (self-signed certificate) for 10.0.1.6->192.168.0.4:8443 and 10.0.1.4->192.168.0.5:443, and the weird/dpd records are SMB (445) and high-port anomalies. Nothing in this window indicates a host in promiscuous mode or a passive sniffer.

summary: While hunting for sniffing tools I found the actual intrusion tooling, which is outbound C2 rather than packet capture: on nashua.dmevals.local, user pbeesly, C:\Windows\Temp\python.exe was launched repeatedly (03:11:40Z, 03:12:46Z, 03:13:49Z, 03:15:03Z) with parent C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe, and then made 348 outbound connections, all to 192.168.0.4:8443 from 10.0.1.6 (e.g. source port 60048 at 03:15:05Z). On scranton.dmevals.local the same user pbeesly ran a hidden, execution-policy-bypassing PowerShell command that decodes a bitmap (monkey.png) into shellcode and IEXs it. These are credential-access/C2-adjacent behaviours, but neither process performs promiscuous-mode capture or writes packet captures, so they do not constitute T1040 network sniffing.

PowerShell opened a full-access handle to lsass.exe and created a remote thread in it on scranton.dmevals.local
summary: On 2020-05-02 at 03:05:16.623Z on scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell.exe (PID 2976, process GUID {47ab858c-e1e4-5eac-b803-000000000400}) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and a CallTrace ending in UNKNOWN(000001996D252982) — i.e. code not backed by a known module. In the same second a second handle with GrantedAccess 0x1fffff was taken, and Sysmon EventID 8 recorded a CreateRemoteThread from that same PowerShell PID into lsass.exe (NewThreadId 912, StartAddress 0x00000117610E0000, StartModule '-', StartFunction '-'). Full-access process handles plus an unbacked remote thread in lsass is the classic credential-API-hooking / in-memory credential theft pattern. This PowerShell activity sits in the same session as the attacker tooling on the host: user pbeesly's script blocks in C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1 include Invoke-ScreenCapture (03:05:53) and Invoke-Exfil, which compresses the Downloads folder with password 'lolol' and copies it to \\192.168.0.4\webdav using hardcoded credentials (03:08:02). By contrast, the other lsass handles in the dataset are benign: svchost.exe via lsm.dll (0x101001), wininit/csrss (0x1fffff, basesrv/CSRSRV), WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe and AntimalwareConfig.exe via CorperfmonExt.dll (0x1400), and a csrss.exe CreateRemoteThread into lsass whose StartFunction is CtrlRoutine in KERNELBASE.dll (console control, benign).

title: Invoke-ScreenCapture PowerShell function repeatedly captured the desktop on scranton.dmevals.local
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PowerShell script block b91c2ae7-3a03-49df-8d2a-4c42fc79df56 (EventID 4104, user pbeesly, path C:\Program Files\SysinternalsSuite\psversion.ps1, 2020-05-02T03:05:53Z) defines function Invoke-ScreenCapture, which starts a background job looping forever, uses System.Windows.Forms/System.Drawing CopyFromScreen to grab the full virtual screen and saves each capture as a random-named .bmp in $env:USERPROFILE\Downloads every 300 seconds. A second script block (0365cb7f-22ef-47e4-ad96-230ddc962939, 03:05:59Z) contains the same System.Windows.Forms/System.Drawing screen-capture body. This is GUI input/screen capture of the user's desktop, collected into the same Downloads folder that the Invoke-Exfil function later archives and uploads to \\192.168.0.4\webdav. No fake credential prompt was observed: the only credential/consent command-line hits were three legitimate consent.exe process creations.

title: No keylogging activity found
summary: No keylogger indicators were observed in any dataset. Searches for GetAsyncKeyState, SetWindowsHookEx and 'keylog' in PowerShell script blocks, Sysmon process command lines and windows.other messages returned zero hits, as did handle/access queries for keyboard objects in windows.security. The only keyboard-related registry writes (Sysmon EventID 13) are Windows keyboard-layout and TERMINPUT_BUS device-enumeration keys under HKU\.DEFAULT and HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Enum, which are normal OS behaviour. The lsass access described under T1056.004 is a credential-memory path, not keystroke capture.

title: No web portal / web-shell credential capture found
summary: No evidence of web portal capture. Searches for IIS/appcmd/wwwroot command lines, 4663 access to wwwroot/inetpub, PowerShell WebAdministration/wwwroot/inetpub script blocks and windows.other messages mentioning wwwroot/inetpub all returned zero hits. The only file creations matching login/logon/portal names are Sysinternals tools (Autologon.exe, logonsessions.exe) downloaded by pbeesly plus Windows netlogon.ftl and the Netlogon operational event log. Zeek HTTP traffic in its separate (non-overlapping) window went only to url.domain 192.168.0.4, with no login/logon/signin URLs.

The credential theft that did occur on this network (see T1110.002 finding) was memory/handle based, not password-guessing based.

title: Credential dumping on scranton: hidden-window PowerShell stager opened lsass with full access (0x1FFFFF)
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, PID 2976 was created at 2020-05-02T02:58:44Z as powershell.exe running with -noni -noexit -ep bypass -window hidden and an encoded command that decodes a System.Drawing bitmap from C:\Users\pbeesly\Downloads\monkey.png and IEXes the extracted bytes (steganographic loader), under user pbeesly. At 2020-05-02T03:05:16.623Z and 03:05:16.654Z that same process (SourceProcessId 2976, SourceImage C:\windows\system32\WindowsPowerShell\v1.0\PowerShell.exe) opened a handle to C:\windows\system32\lsass.exe (TargetProcessId 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1F3FFF and then 0x1FFFFF — full-access PROCESS_ALL_ACCESS, the access pattern used to read lsass memory and extract credentials/hashes for offline cracking. This is the only PowerShell-to-lsass access in the dataset with such access rights; the other 322 lsass accesses are svchost.exe/Azure telemetry agents with 0x1000/0x1400. In the same session pbeesly also ran Get-PrivateKeys (exporting all LocalMachine certificates to .pfx with password 'saribas') and Invoke-Exfil (7-Zip of the Downloads folder to %APPDATA%\OfficeSupplies.7z), and made repeated 4648 explicit-credential logons to nashua.dmevals.local via C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe. The 4656 handle requests on SAM/SECURITY/ntds.dit objects were all issued by lsass.exe itself (10 events), i.e. normal, and the 3 file-creation hits for *SECURITY* were only Prefetch files for SecurityHealthHost/Service/Systray — no hive or ntds.dit copy was observed.

title: No password spraying: 4648 explicit-credential logons are single-account admin/PSEXEC use, not many-accounts-one-password
summary: All 15 4648 events use the same account, pbeesly: 9 on scranton.dmevals.local and nashua.dmevals.local (5 and 4) plus 6 machine/service accounts (DWM-1, DWM-2, UMFD-0/1/2, SCRANTON$) generated by winlogon.exe, wininit.exe and taskhostw.exe at 23:19-23:20, which is normal Windows desktop/session behaviour. The pbeesly 4648s on nashua come from C:\Windows\PSEXESVC.exe (PsExec service) and on scranton from svchost.exe with source.ip 10.0.1.6 / 172.18.39.2. Spraying requires one password tried against many distinct accounts; here only one user account is ever presented, so this is lateral movement with already-obtained credentials rather than spraying. Note this activity is still attacker-driven (see T1110.002) but does not match T1110.003.

title: No credential stuffing: no failed authentications and no stuffing script observed
summary: Credential stuffing requires many authentication attempts using lists of stolen credentials, which would surface as repeated 4625/4771 failures. windows.security contains zero 4625 events and only one 4776 (a success for pbeesly from 10.0.1.4 on newyork). The four 4104 script blocks matching *Credential*/*Password*/*Login* contain no credential-list iteration: they are a certificate-export function, a 7-Zip exfiltration function, and two benign helper/help texts. No stuffing tooling or authentication loop was found.

title: No MFA/smart-card interception artifacts; credential theft on scranton was certificate private-key export plus LSASS access
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local, user pbeesly's PowerShell session (spawned 02:56:14 from cmd.exe, itself spawned by C:\ProgramData\victim\...cod.3aka3.scr) ran a credential-access chain: at 03:04:56 it defined and invoked Get-PrivateKeys, which enumerates cert:\LocalMachine and exports certificates to .pfx files in the user's Downloads folder using the hardcoded password 'saribas'; at 03:05:16 the same PowerShell process (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe (PID 736) with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and 0x1fffff (full access, consistent with credential dumping). This is credential/certificate theft, but nothing in the retrieved data shows interception of MFA: no smart-card registry changes (C130 zero hits), no smart-card/MFA provider events, and the only 'Credential' string in windows.other is a routine 'Credential Guard configuration: 0x0, 0' message on scranton at 03:19:09. The 4648 explicit-credential logons are pbeesly authenticating to NASHUA via PSEXESVC.exe (03:11-03:15) and machine-account/DWM/UMFD logons on scranton during a reboot at 03:19-03:20 — lateral movement and normal system behaviour, not MFA interception. The wsmprovhost.exe LSASS access on nashua at 03:09:29 (0x1f3fff) has a PowerShell/System.ni.dll call trace consistent with PowerShell remoting enumeration rather than a dump tool. T1111 itself is therefore not observed; the underlying credential-access activity is real and malicious in context.

title: WebDAV forced authentication from 10.0.1.4 to 192.168.0.4 after SMB fallback (DavClnt / Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir)
summary: In the Zeek window (2020-04-30 00:32:14–00:35:25Z), host 10.0.1.4 attempted SMB to 192.168.0.4 on TCP 445 and 139 ten times, all rejected (conn_state REJ, 0 bytes). It then immediately switched to HTTP on port 80 to the same host, where the client identified itself as 'DavClnt' (OPTIONS /, 403) and then 'Microsoft-WebDAV-MiniRedir/10.0.18362' for 61 requests. The WebDAV session shows the classic forced-authentication handshake: repeated PROPFIND to /webdav and /webdav/ answered with 401 challenges followed by 207 Multi-Status, then PROPFIND/PUT/LOCK/PROPPATCH/UNLOCK against a lure file '/webdav/OfficeSupplies.7z' (PUT 201/204, LOCK 200, PROPPATCH 207, UNLOCK 204). The 401-then-success pattern on each method is the server soliciting NTLM credentials from the Windows WebClient service, i.e. the victim host being coerced into authenticating to an attacker-controlled WebDAV server. All 62 HTTP requests in the dataset went to 192.168.0.4 and 61 of 62 used the WebDAV MiniRedir user agent, so this is not normal browsing traffic. The Windows-side SMB connections in the 2020-05-02 window are unrelated: all 66 Sysmon event.code 3 records on 445/139 come from process.executable 'System' (SYSTEM) to internal hosts 10.0.0.4 and a link-local IPv6 address, consistent with normal domain controller traffic. No .scf/.url/.library-ms lure files were created; the only .lnk creations were Explorer writing Recent shortcuts for pbeesly and a powershell.exe-created hostui.lnk in the StartUp folder on scranton.dmevals.local, which is persistence rather than forced authentication.

title: PowerShell on SCRANTON opened LSASS and winlogon with full-access masks (0x1FFFFF/0x1F3FFF) during a pbeesly intrusion chain
summary: On scranton.dmevals.local the user pbeesly ran a hands-on-keyboard PowerShell intrusion: a malicious screen-saver C:\ProgramData\victim\cod.3aka3.scr launched from explorer.exe spawned cmd.exe/powershell.exe, followed by Invoke-Discovery, Invoke-Persistence, Invoke-ScreenCapture, Invoke-Exfil (7-Zip archive with password 'lolol'), sdelete64.exe wiping artifacts, and Invoke-SeaDukeStage -ComputerName NASHUA. At 2020-05-02T03:05:16 PowerShell.exe (PID 2976) opened lsass.exe with GrantedAccess 0x1f3fff and then 0x1fffff, and in the same second opened winlogon.exe, LogonUI.exe, dwm.exe and multiple svchost.exe with 0x1fffff — a full-access credential-theft pattern (LSASS + interactive logon session memory) with an UNKNOWN call-trace module, not a signed security product. This is the credential-access step of the intrusion, immediately preceding lateral movement to NASHUA (wsmprovhost.exe on nashua opened lsass.exe with 0x1f3fff at 03:09:29 after pbeesly's Kerberos logon and SeDebugPrivilege 4672 events).

title: Routine LSASS handle activity by svchost.exe, Azure antimalware/telemetry and OS processes is benign
summary: The bulk of the 326 LSASS process-access events are low-privilege handles: svchost.exe with 0x1000 (216 on scranton, 30 on newyork, 28 on nashua, 12 on utica), AntimalwareConfig.exe and WindowsAzureTelemetryService.exe with 0x1400, and OS-internal accesses by wininit.exe/csrss.exe/svchost.exe at 03:18-03:19 on scranton (0x1fffff/0x1000000/0x3000/0x101001) consistent with normal service and session management. No credential-dumping command lines (procdump/comsvcs/MiniDump) were found in process creation, no lsass/MiniDump strings in PowerShell script blocks or windows.other messages, and the Kerberos events (4768/4769 for pbeesly and SCRANTON$) are ordinary ticket requests accompanying the logons. The only anomalous LSASS access is the PowerShell/wsmprovhost full-access pattern reported separately.

title: No web session cookie theft observed; browser cookie/credential stores never accessed
summary: Hunted T1539 across windows.sysmon, windows.security, windows.powershell and windows.other for the 2020-05-02 02:55-03:28Z window on scranton/newyork/nashua/utica.dmevals.local. No browser cookie or credential store was read or copied. (1) Sysmon event 10 (process access) shows zero events where win.TargetImage matches chrome/firefox/msedge/iexplore/brave/opera, so no process opened a browser with cookie-read access. (2) Sysmon event 11 file creations matching cookies/login data/user data/mozilla/profiles returned a single hit, svchost.exe writing C:\Windows\ServiceProfiles\LocalService\AppData\Local\Packages\warp_jit_db4a1097-...\AC\INetCookies - an OS package container path, not a browser profile. The 162-hit C149 result was a wildcard false positive: the buckets are lastalive0.dat/lastalive1.dat and GroupPolicy DataStore paths written by svchost.exe. (3) Security 4663 object-access events on cookies/login data/user data/mozilla paths: zero. (4) The 4 C148 4688 hits are all C:\Windows\System32\SearchProtocolHost.exe (parent SearchIndexer.exe) whose command line merely contains the literal string "Mozilla/4.0 (compatible; MSIE 6.0; Windows NT; MS Search 4.0 Robot)" - the Windows Search indexer user-agent, not browser access.
